title: Low air warnings
why: Your truck warns you when air pressure in the service tank gets low. Knowing the warning point tells you when to act.

key_facts.label: Warning comes on
key_facts.text: Before service reservoir pressure falls below 60 psi, or half the governor cut-out pressure if that is lower

key_facts.label: Which number applies
key_facts.text: The lower of the two

title: Brake system basics
why: Every commercial vehicle needs brakes that can stop it and hold it. The rules say how the brake systems must be set up.

key_facts.label: Overall rule
key_facts.text: Brakes must be able to stop and hold the vehicle or combination

key_facts.label: Where brakes go
key_facts.text: Brakes must act on all wheels, with a few listed exceptions

key_facts.label: One valve
key_facts.text: One application valve operates all service brakes on a power-braked vehicle

key_facts.label: Emergency brake
key_facts.text: The driver must be able to apply it from the normal seat while belted

title: Towing and emergency braking
why: If a trailer comes loose or air leaks, the truck must keep its air and the trailer must stop. Special valves and controls make that happen.

key_facts.label: Tractor protection valve
key_facts.text: Closes by itself when towing-unit air falls to between 20 and 45 psi

key_facts.label: Two controls
key_facts.text: One automatic and one manual control the seated driver can reach

key_facts.label: If trailer breaks away
key_facts.text: The towing vehicle's service brakes must still stop it

key_facts.label: Relay valves
key_facts.text: Trailers use no-bleed-back relay emergency valves

title: Air tanks and brake lines
why: Air tanks and brake lines must stay in good shape. A leak or kink in the wrong place can cost you your brakes.

key_facts.label: Drain valve
key_facts.text: Each air reservoir needs a drain valve you can open by hand

key_facts.label: Check valves
key_facts.text: They protect against pressure loss from a leak between the tank and its source

key_facts.label: Tubing and hoses
key_facts.text: Secured against chafing and kinking, and kept away from the exhaust and other heat

key_facts.label: Coiled tubing
key_facts.text: Only between a towing vehicle and a towed vehicle (or an adjustable axle subframe)

title: Gauges and brake adjusters
why: Your gauge and warning signal tell you what the air system is doing. Automatic adjusters and indicators help keep your brakes in adjustment.

key_facts.label: Gauge and warning
key_facts.text: Air-braked vehicles must have a pressure gauge and a warning signal

key_facts.label: What the gauge shows
key_facts.text: The air pressure available for braking

key_facts.label: Automatic adjusters
key_facts.text: Required on air-braked CMVs made on or after October 20, 1994

key_facts.label: Adjustment indicator
key_facts.text: Shows when the service brakes are under-adjusted

title: Commercial learner's permit
why: A commercial learner's permit (CLP) lets you practice driving a commercial vehicle on public roads. You must have a CDL holder beside you the whole time.

key_facts.label: How long it lasts
key_facts.text: No more than one year from the first issue date, unless you retake the knowledge tests

key_facts.label: Wait for the skills test
key_facts.text: You may not take the CDL skills test in the first 14 days

key_facts.label: Who rides with you
key_facts.text: A CDL holder with the right group and endorsements, seated next to you in a truck

key_facts.label: No hazmat
key_facts.text: A CLP holder may not drive a vehicle that carries hazardous materials

title: Disqualifications
why: Some offenses take away your right to drive a commercial vehicle. Knowing how long each one lasts helps you protect your license.

key_facts.label: First major offense
key_facts.text: 1 year, or 3 years if you were hauling hazardous materials

key_facts.label: Second major offense
key_facts.text: Disqualified for life, from a separate incident

key_facts.label: Serious traffic violations
key_facts.text: 60 days for a second in 3 years, 120 days for a third

key_facts.label: Speeding
key_facts.text: Serious when 15 mph or more over the limit

title: Alcohol and fatigue
why: Alcohol and tiredness both slow your reaction time. The federal rules set clear limits for both.

key_facts.label: Before duty
key_facts.text: No alcohol within 4 hours before going on duty or driving

key_facts.label: On duty
key_facts.text: No measured alcohol while on duty or in control of a CMV

key_facts.label: After a violation
key_facts.text: Placed out of service for 24 hours

key_facts.label: Tired or ill
key_facts.text: Do not drive if fatigue or illness makes driving unsafe

title: Phones and seat belts
why: Phones take your eyes and hands off the job. Federal rules limit phone use in a CMV and require seat belts.

key_facts.label: Texting
key_facts.text: Not allowed while driving, and driving includes stops in traffic with the engine running

key_facts.label: Hand-held phone
key_facts.text: Not allowed while driving, except to reach police or emergency services

key_facts.label: Safe stop
key_facts.text: Not driving once safely parked where the vehicle can remain stopped

key_facts.label: Seat belt
key_facts.text: Wear the installed belt whenever you drive a CMV

title: Hours of service
why: Tired drivers cause crashes. Hours-of-service rules limit how long a property-carrying driver can drive and work.

key_facts.label: Before you drive
key_facts.text: 10 consecutive hours off duty

key_facts.label: Driving limits
key_facts.text: 11 hours of driving inside a 14-hour window

key_facts.label: Break
key_facts.text: A 30-minute break once you pass 8 hours of driving

key_facts.label: Weekly limits
key_facts.text: 60 hours in 7 days, or 70 hours in 8 days; a 34-hour off-duty period restarts the count

title: Inspections and reports
why: You are responsible for knowing your vehicle is safe. Federal rules cover what you check, what you write down and how often the vehicle is inspected.

key_facts.label: Before driving
key_facts.text: Be satisfied that key parts work, including brakes, steering, lights, tires and coupling devices

key_facts.label: End of day
key_facts.text: Write a vehicle inspection report for each vehicle you drove

key_facts.label: Records
key_facts.text: The carrier keeps the report and repair certification for 3 months

key_facts.label: Periodic inspection
key_facts.text: Every CMV must pass an inspection at least once in 12 months

title: Cargo and tire checks
why: Loose cargo and worn tires cause many roadside problems. The rules say when to check cargo and how much tread tires need.

key_facts.label: First cargo check
key_facts.text: Within the first 50 miles of a trip

key_facts.label: Re-check cargo
key_facts.text: After a duty status change, 3 hours or 150 miles, whichever comes first

key_facts.label: Steering tires
key_facts.text: At least 4/32 inch of tread

key_facts.label: Other tires
key_facts.text: At least 2/32 inch of tread

title: Stopped vehicles and emergency gear
why: A stopped truck is a hazard to other drivers. You need to warn traffic fast and carry the right emergency equipment.

key_facts.label: First step
key_facts.text: Turn on the hazard flashers when you stop on the road or shoulder

key_facts.label: Warning devices
key_facts.text: Place them as soon as possible, within 10 minutes

key_facts.label: Where to place
key_facts.text: About 10 feet, 100 feet ahead and 100 feet behind; on divided roads 200 feet, 100 feet and within 10 feet of the rear

key_facts.label: Fire extinguisher
key_facts.text: One rated 10 B:C if you carry placarded hazmat

title: Coupling devices
why: A tractor and trailer are held together by a coupling device. The rules say how it must lock and what backup is needed.

key_facts.label: Fifth wheel lock
key_facts.text: Must stop the halves from separating unless a positive manual release is used

key_facts.label: Tracking
key_facts.text: The trailer may deviate no more than 3 inches to either side of the towing vehicle's path

key_facts.label: Safety devices
key_facts.text: Chains, cables or a bridle connect a full trailer to the towing vehicle's frame

key_facts.label: Safety device strength
key_facts.text: At least the gross weight of the vehicle being towed

title: Trailer lights and guards
why: Other drivers need to see your trailer and stay clear of its rear. Required lights, reflective tape and rear guards help with that.

key_facts.label: Lamp colors
key_facts.text: Stop lamps and tail lamps must be red; amber stop or tail lamps are not allowed

key_facts.label: Conspicuity
key_facts.text: Trailers 80 inches or wider, over 10,000 pounds GVWR, made on or after December 1, 1993 need it

key_facts.label: Rear impact guard
key_facts.text: Trailers made on or after January 26, 1998 with 10,000 pounds GVWR or more generally need one

key_facts.label: Guard height
key_facts.text: Bottom edge no more than 22 inches off the ground

title: Trailer brakes and ABS
why: Trailer brakes must work even if the trailer comes loose. Newer rigs also have ABS lamps that warn you of a problem.

key_facts.label: Breakaway
key_facts.text: A trailer's required brakes must apply automatically and immediately

key_facts.label: Hold time
key_facts.text: On trailers with fewer than three axles, they stay applied at least 15 minutes

key_facts.label: Surge brakes
key_facts.text: Allowed on a trailer up to 12,000 pounds GVWR if no more than 1.75 times the towing vehicle's GVWR

key_facts.label: ABS
key_facts.text: Air-braked trailers made on or after March 1, 1998 need an exterior ABS lamp

title: Shipping papers
why: Shipping papers tell you and first responders what is in your load. They must be written correctly and kept where they can be found fast.

key_facts.label: Description order
key_facts.text: ID number, proper shipping name, hazard class, packing group

key_facts.label: Quantity
key_facts.text: Total quantity with a unit of measure

key_facts.label: While driving
key_facts.text: Within reach when belted in, and visible or in the driver's door holder

key_facts.label: Out of the cab
key_facts.text: In the driver's door holder or on the driver's seat

title: Placards
why: Placards warn other people about your load. Whether you need one depends on the hazard class and how much you carry.

key_facts.label: Any amount
key_facts.text: Explosives 1.1 to 1.3, poison gas, dangerous when wet, poison inhalation hazard, and Radioactive Yellow III

key_facts.label: Other classes
key_facts.text: Placards are needed at 1,001 pounds total gross weight or more

key_facts.label: Bulk packaging
key_facts.text: Placard any amount on each side and each end

key_facts.label: DANGEROUS placard
key_facts.text: May replace separate placards for non-bulk loads of two or more categories

title: Emergency response information
why: If there is a spill or fire, responders need to know what to do. Emergency response information must go with every shipment and be easy to reach.

key_facts.label: What it includes
key_facts.text: Hazards, fire and explosion risks, spill steps and first aid

key_facts.label: Language
key_facts.text: Printed legibly in English

key_facts.label: Where it can be
key_facts.text: On a shipping paper, in another document, or in a separate document tied to the shipping paper entry

key_facts.label: Access
key_facts.text: Immediately accessible to drivers for use in incidents

title: Loading and mixing
why: Some hazardous materials can react if they ride together. The segregation table shows which ones must stay apart.

key_facts.label: X on the table
key_facts.text: Materials may not be loaded, carried or stored together in the same vehicle

key_facts.label: O on the table
key_facts.text: Not stored together unless separated so a leak would not mix them

key_facts.label: Cyanides and acids
key_facts.text: Not carried together if hydrogen cyanide could form

key_facts.label: Class 8 liquids
key_facts.text: Not loaded above or next to Class 4 or Class 5 materials

title: Parking, fuel and tires
why: Part 397 sets driver rules for hazmat loads: who watches the vehicle, where to park, no smoking, safe fueling and tire checks.

key_facts.label: Attended
key_facts.text: Person in charge is on the vehicle awake, or within 100 feet with it in clear view

key_facts.label: Parking
key_facts.text: Not on or within 5 feet of the traveled part of a public road

key_facts.label: Smoking
key_facts.text: No lit cigarettes, cigars or pipes on or within 25 feet of certain loads

key_facts.label: Tires
key_facts.text: Check every tire at the start of each trip and each time the vehicle is parked
